# Introduction

This report combines the main results from the previous assignments.
We first give a short overview of the data, then summarize the main
descriptive analyses, and finally present the regression analysis.

# Data Overview

The project uses TikTok-related data from both a SQLite database and
several CSV files. Across the assignments, we worked with information
on videos, impressions, sessions, users, and watch events.

## Video overview

```{r}
con <- dbConnect(SQLite(), here("Data", "tiktok_students.sqlite"))
videos <- dbReadTable(con, "video_view")
dbDisconnect(con)

overview <- videos %>%
  summarise(
    n_videos = n(),
    n_creators = n_distinct(creator_id),
    avg_length = mean(video_length_sec, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_watch_rate = mean(watch_rate, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

overview
```

## Short vs long videos

```{r}
length_groups <- videos %>%
  mutate(length_group = ifelse(video_length_sec < 30, "short", "long")) %>%
  group_by(length_group) %>%
  summarise(
    videos_n = n(),
    watch_rate_avg = mean(watch_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    watch_share_avg = mean(avg_watch_share, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

length_groups
```

Short and long videos had very similar average watch rate and watch share.
So based on this descriptive comparison, video length alone does not seem
to make a clear difference in audience retention.

# Descriptive Analyses

## Impressions

The impressions dataset originally contained 95,737 rows. We found 786
fully duplicated rows and removed them, leaving 94,951 rows. The
`mission_ids` variable also had 13,926 missing values.

After removing the exact duplicates, 161 repeated `impression_id`
values were still present. These were kept because the other variables
differed, meaning they likely represented separate impressions rather
than data errors.

Most impressions came from the `preferred_new` feed (51.6%), followed
by `explore` (31.4%) and `known` (17.0%).

# Regression Analysis

The final part of the project studies whether having seen a creator
before is related to watch time.

```{r}
source(here("src", "Assignment3", "regression_sql.R"))
```

The regression uses data from `watch_logs` and `video_view`. Two main
variables are created: `seen_before`, which indicates whether a user
has already seen the same creator, and `long_video`, which indicates
whether a video is longer than the median video length.

We estimated four models:
- Model 1: watch time explained by prior creator exposure
- Model 2: adds video length
- Model 3: includes the interaction between prior exposure and video length
- Model 4: repeats the interaction model using log-transformed watch time

## Model output

```

```

## Regression Results

In Model 1, `seen_before` has a negative coefficient of -0.305. This means
that users watched about 0.3 seconds less, on average, when they had seen
the same creator before. The effect is statistically significant, although
it is very small.

After adding video length in Model 2, the coefficient for `seen_before`
remains negative (-0.315). Long videos are associated with about 5.73
seconds more watch time than short videos.

Model 3 includes an interaction between prior exposure and video length.
The interaction coefficient is negative (-0.111) and statistically
significant. This suggests that the negative relationship between prior
creator exposure and watch time is slightly stronger for long videos.

However, in Model 4, where watch time is log-transformed, the interaction
term is no longer significant (p = 0.703). This means that the interaction
effect is not very robust across model specifications.

# Conclusion

The descriptive analyses showed several patterns in TikTok viewing
behaviour across videos, impressions, sessions, users, and watch events.

The regression analysis showed that previous exposure to the same creator
was associated with slightly lower watch time, while longer videos were
associated with higher watch time. The interaction between these two
variables was statistically significant in the model using raw watch time,
but not in the log-transformed model.

The size of the prior-exposure effect was small, and the models explained
only a limited part of the variation in watch time. The results therefore
show associations in this dataset rather than strong evidence of a causal
relationship.

# Limitations

This project has a few limitations. Some datasets needed cleaning, and
some variables contained missing values or duplicate records. Also, not
all potentially important factors are observed in the data.

Because of this, the results should be understood as a structured
analysis of the available data rather than a complete explanation of
user behaviour.
